h1: Permits, inspections and a file that closes
hero_sub: Permit applications, HVHZ product approvals, inspections and sign-offs across Miami-Dade and Broward, plus the unglamorous work of closing out open permits and legalizing what a previous owner never filed. Licensed general contractor, Lic. CGC1539072.
local_heading: One code, two counties, many front desks
intro_paragraphs: Permitting is the part of a high-end project nobody puts on a mood board and everybody remembers. At this level it means a complete drawing set, sealed engineering wherever the structure changes, product approvals matched to the right openings, a permit issued in a licensed contractor's name, and a file that eventually closes. Two kinds of owners call us. The first is planning serious work and wants it legal, insurable and appraisable. The second already has a problem: an open permit from a prior owner, a failed inspection, a recertification notice, or a garage conversion nobody ever filed.

Two things make South Florida different. Miami-Dade and Broward together form the state's High-Velocity Hurricane Zone, so every window, door, skylight and roof assembly in the set has to carry a Miami-Dade Notice of Acceptance or a Florida Product Approval valid in the HVHZ, with anchor details and installation instructions attached. Near salt water the code also gets specific about corrosion-resistant fasteners and connectors. And the counties are not interchangeable: each has its own board of rules and appeals publishing the county amendments and certifying the officials who will review your job, and Miami-Dade's Product Control Section is where the NOAs themselves originate.

We scope permitting the way we scope construction, in writing and before anything moves. A walk-through first, then an honest read of what the work actually triggers, then the right professionals engaged early, architect, structural engineer and surveyor, so the application goes in complete instead of in pieces. Incomplete sets are what turn one review cycle into three. Once the permit issues, inspections are phased and a supervisor from PGX is on site to meet the inspector. The last line on our schedule is not the final coat of paint. It is the final inspection and a permit marked closed.

The rules change every few miles. A Coral Gables exterior answers to the Board of Architects, Miami Beach adds historic review, Fisher Island and the Ponce-Davis pocket file with unincorporated Miami-Dade, the Las Olas isles and Rio Vista go through Fort Lauderdale, and the barrier towns, the condo corridors and the western estate areas each run their own building department. Flood elevation and association approval matter on one street and not on the next. We serve 42 areas across the two counties. Every one of them has a page here naming the authority you will actually deal with.

faqs.q: Does my project actually need a permit?
faqs.a: Almost certainly, if it touches structure, plumbing, electrical, mechanical, windows, doors or the roof. Paint, flooring laid over an existing slab and cabinetry swapped in place generally do not. The gray zone is wider than people expect, and guessing wrong is expensive later, because unpermitted work surfaces during a sale, a refinance or an insurance inspection. We give you a straight answer at the walk-through, in writing, before anyone orders material.

faqs.q: How long does permitting take in Miami-Dade or Broward?
faqs.a: Weeks, not days, and the honest answer depends on scope and on how complete the first submittal is. Interior work with no structural change moves fastest. Anything carrying sealed engineering, flood compliance, design review or a condo board in front of it takes longer, because those approvals run on their own clocks and several of them are sequential rather than parallel. We publish a permitting timeline with the estimate and flag the items nobody controls.

Permit fees are set by the jurisdiction and generally scale with the value of the work, so they are not something a contractor invents, marks up or discounts away. What we do control is the professional side: drawings, engineering, coordination and our own time, all of it inside a fixed written scope agreed before we start. PGX is a high-end contractor and rarely the lowest bid, because we price the whole path to a closed permit rather than the cheerful half of it.

faqs.q: Where do permit files get stuck?
faqs.a: Paperwork, mostly. An incomplete submittal that draws the same comments twice. Product approvals that do not match what was actually ordered. Flood rules, where improvements approach half the building's pre-improvement market value and the entire structure has to be brought into current compliance. And unpermitted work by a previous owner, discovered when the plans meet the county's records. We look for all four before design, not during plan review.

faqs.q: Who handles this day to day?
faqs.a: One team and one phone number. PGX is the licensed general contractor of record, Lic. CGC1539072, so the permit carries our name and the responsibility is ours. We coordinate the architect, engineer and surveyor, file the application, answer plan-review comments, schedule inspections and meet the inspector on site. You are not chasing three consultants and a permit clerk to find out why nothing moved this week.

faqs.q: There is an open permit on the house and we are trying to close. What now?
faqs.a: Start now, not the week of closing. An open or expired permit stays attached to the property, and lenders and title companies do notice. The path is usually to pull the file, see which inspections were never done, reactivate or take assignment of the permit as a licensed contractor, correct whatever the work genuinely needs, and pass the final. Some close quickly. Others uncover work that has to be brought up to current code first, and we tell you which one you have before you promise anyone a date.
